item.base_system: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with random solid solution (RSS) structure
item.intervention: Introduction of chemical short-range order (SRO) to the alloy system
item.processing: MC/MD simulations with 10^2 MC swaps every 10^3 MD steps at 800 K to equilibrate SRO
item.test_conditions: Temperature range 300 to 2000 K; shear stress 0 to 1.0 GPa
item.structure_change: Local chemical ordering established; SRO parameter defined by Warren Cowley order parameter
item.property_change: Screw dislocation mobility decreased (strengthening effect); edge dislocation mobility increased (acceleration)
item.attributed_mechanism: SRO increases the formation energy for a double kink (ΔH_DAPB) for screw dislocations, while it flattens the energy landscape reducing solute drag for edge dislocations
quotes: Short-range order (SRO) is found to play opposite roles in the motion of screw and edge dislocation in RHEAs: it will hinder screw dislocation motion yet accelerate the motion of edges.
The strengthening induced by the presence of the local chemical SRO is found to be highly temperature-dependent; specifically, it is found to decrease at high homologous temperatures.

In the high-stress regime, the influence of SRO on the motion of the edge dislocation is the direct opposite from that for the screw dislocation, in that the velocity of the edge dislocations is enhanced in the SRO sample compared to that in the RSS sample.

item.processing: MD simulations comparing RSS and SRO samples
item.test_conditions: Low-stress regime at temperatures 300 to 2000 K
item.structure_change: SRO sample shows a flatter energy landscape compared to RSS

item.intervention: Varying temperature from 300 K to 2000 K
item.processing: MD simulations to determine critical friction stress
item.test_conditions: Stress ramped to find velocity thresholds (0.2 Å/ps for screw, 1.0 Å/ps for edge)
item.structure_change: Critical stress for screw dislocation fits exponential decay; edge dislocation fits linear decay
item.property_change: Critical friction stress for screw dislocation decays at a much higher rate (1.3 GPa drop) than edge dislocation (140 MPa drop)
item.attributed_mechanism: Different mechanisms: kink-pair nucleation barrier for screws vs. solute drag for edges
quotes: Figure 8a shows the critical stress as a function of temperature for the screw dislocation in the RSS RHEA, which are fit well by an exponential decay curve, whereas in Fig. 8b , the critical stress for the edge dislocation is well fit by a function that decreases linearly with temperature.
Moreover, the critical stress for the screw dislocation is more sensitive to the increment of temperature and, as such, decays at a much higher rate compared with the edge dislocation.

According to our simulation data, from 300 to 2000 K the critical friction stress decreases by 140 MPa for the edge dislocation, whereas the decrease is almost an order of magnitude larger at 1.3 GPa for the screw dislocation.

Quote: "Figure 8a shows the critical stress as a function of temperature for the screw dislocation in the RSS RHEA, which are fit well by an exponential decay curve, whereas in Fig. 8b , the critical stress for the edge dislocation is well fit by a function that decreases linearly with temperature."

item.intervention: Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) development
item.processing: Grid search for hyperparameters: R_cut = 4.7 Å, lev_max = 14
item.test_conditions: Reproducing elastic constants and stacking fault energies
item.structure_change: Construction of contracted rotationally invariant local environment descriptors
item.property_change: Accurate potential for simulating dislocation mobility in RHEA
item.attributed_mechanism: MTP constructs polynomial regression between potential energy surface and moment tensor descriptors
quotes: In this work, we adopted the grid search method to examine the choice of hyperparameters by evaluating the performance on reproducing the basic materials properties, e.g., elastic constants and stacking fault energies.

The MTP essentially constructs contracted rotationally invariant local environment descriptors for each atom in the system and builds a polynomial regressed correlation between the potential energy surface (PES) and these descriptors.
